item.title: Criminals attack French postal operator subsidiary, grab contact details of 22M people
item.description: The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say. La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste. Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer. According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year. The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September. The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days. A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October. Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend. Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data. However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently. In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions. According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates. Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years. La Poste said in a statement to The Register : "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients." The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year. On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year. item.title: Supreme Court Ends Custodia Bank’s Fight for a Fed Master Account, Leaving the Fed Free to Deny Crypto Banks Access
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Supreme Court Ends Custodia Bank’s Fight for a Fed Master Account, Leaving the Fed Free to Deny Crypto Banks Access The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied Custodia Bank’s petition to review the Federal Reserve’s refusal to give the Wyoming bitcoin bank a master account, ending chief executive Caitlin Long’s years-long fight for direct access to the central bank’s payment rails. The case, Custodia Bank, Inc. v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, No. 26-62, is listed under “certiorari denied” on the Court’s Monday order list . The denial leaves in place a Tenth Circuit ruling that regional Federal Reserve Banks have discretion to reject even eligible applicants, and it closes the last court path Custodia had to force the Fed’s hand. A master account is a bank’s account at a Federal Reserve Bank, and the entry point to Fedwire and other payment services. Without one, a state-chartered bank has to rely on a correspondent institution to move money. Eligible, then turned away Custodia is a Wyoming special purpose depository institution, a charter that bars it from making loans and requires dollar deposits to be fully reserved in liquid assets. After receiving that charter, it applied for a master account at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City in October 2020. In January 2021, the Kansas City Fed confirmed the bank was legally eligible and told it there were “no showstoppers.” In August 2021, Custodia also applied for Federal Reserve membership. While those requests sat pending, the Board of Governors in August 2022 published guidelines for evaluating master-account applications. The rules put firms that are neither federally insured nor supervised by a federal banking agency into “Tier 3,” the group that “generally receive[s] the strictest level of review.” Custodia fell into that bucket. On January 27, 2023, the Kansas City Fed denied the master account, citing an “unprecedented” business model “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities” and concluding the risks were “highly likely” to be “inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The same day, the Board denied Custodia’s membership application, saying approval “would be inconsistent with the financial, managerial, and corporate powers factors.” The last Custodia appeal fails Custodia had already sued the Fed and the Kansas City Fed in June 2022 over the delay. On March 29, 2024, U.S. District Judge Scott W. Skavdahl in Wyoming ruled that the Federal Reserve Act gives Reserve Banks discretion to grant or deny master accounts, dismissed Custodia’s Administrative Procedure Act claim for lack of a final agency action, and granted the Kansas City Fed summary judgment. The Tenth Circuit affirmed on October 31, 2025, in a 2-1 decision Bitcoin Magazine covered at the time. item.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
item.description: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Jim Mirandy, quality assurance specialist at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, poses for a photograph at the High Pressure Gas Facility on Nov. 10, 2026. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. item.title: [PHOTOS] Nigeria Re-Elected To Council Of International Telecommunication Union
item.description: Nigeria has been re-elected to the Council of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) at the ongoing conference in Doha, Qatar. With this development, Nigeria retains its seat on the council for the term 2027-2030. As part of Nigeria’s campaign for re-election, the Ambassador to Qatar Mahmood Yakubu (right) had a bilateral meeting with Mr. Jijun Xiong, China’s Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology and Leader of the Chinese delegation to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) conference (Doha 2026). Established in 1865 with headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, the ITU is the United Nations specialised agency for information and communication technologies (ICTs). It brings together 194 member states and over 1,000 sector members, which include companies, universities and international organisations. Nigeria became a member in 1961. Nigeria’s participation was coordinated by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu. The Nigerian delegation was led by the Minister of Communication, Innovation and Digital Economy, Bosun Tijani. With this development, Nigeria retains its seat on the council for the term 2027-2030. Nigeria’s Ambassador to the State of Qatar, Mahmood Yakubu, served as the Deputy Head of Delegation, supported by the Executive Vice Chairman of the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), Aminu Maida; Nigeria’s Permanent Mission to Geneva, led by Innocent Imejuo; officials of the Ministry of Communication (NCC) and staff of the Nigerian Embassy in Doha. item.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
item.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.” Continue reading...

item.title: Euclid space telescope discovers its 1st comet | Space photo of the day for Nov. 16, 2026
item.description: null The comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) discovered by the Euclid mission. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026) The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short. What is it? (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24. "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement . Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us. An close up view of comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) Why is it incredible? Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

item.title: Hong Kong to License Crypto Dealers and Custodians by Year-End
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Hong Kong to License Crypto Dealers and Custodians by Year-End Hong Kong will introduce a bill before the end of the year to bring crypto dealers, advisers, asset managers and custodians under a licensing regime, Financial Secretary Paul Chan said Monday, even as the city has approved only two of 36 first-round applicants to issue stablecoins. Chan delivered the remarks in a keynote at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum in Hong Kong. “Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter, extending licensing to those who deal in, advise on, manage and act as custodians of digital assets,” he said. The plan would amend the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, expanding a regime that now covers virtual asset trading platforms, the government told the Legislative Council on Nov. 4. A tight gate for stablecoins “On stablecoins, we have moved forward step by step. Of the 36 applicants in the first round, two received licences in April, and both have since launched Hong Kong dollar stablecoins,” Chan said. He said the emphasis is on “genuine use cases and credible business models,” citing cross-border payments as an example. The Stablecoins Ordinance took effect in August 2025. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority granted the two issuer licenses this April, the government said in that earlier Legislative Council reply. Chan did not name the two issuers or say when a further application round might open. The low approval rate is the point. Hong Kong is trying to build a regulated digital-asset market without opening the door to every issuer that applies. Same activity, same regulation “Our principle is simple: same activity, same risks, same regulation,” Chan said. On tokenisation, he said funds offered to the public in Hong Kong have grown about seven-fold in a year, and that since last month two tokenised money market funds have traded around the clock on a licensed platform. “Our approach is consistent: the same requirements as for conventional products, with additional safeguards for the new risks.” Those figures line up with a fuller count the government gave on Nov. 4. As of the end of September, the Securities and Futures Commission had authorized 17 retail tokenised products, including 13 tokenised money market funds, with about HK$10.3 billion in assets in their tokenised classes. Two of those money market funds began round-the-clock secondary trading on licensed platforms on Oct. 26. “Above all, we are firm on one point: Decentralisation does not mean less accountability,” Chan said. Completing the perimeter Hong Kong already licenses virtual asset trading platforms. The new bill is meant to pull dealing, advisory, management and custody work into the same ordinance, a step the government has framed as streamlining the legal perimeter rather than writing a new one from scratch. item.title: Microsoft Outlook outage blamed after 15 injured in hotel pool chlorine incident
item.description: Most victims of last week's Microsoft outage lost access to their email, but 15 unlucky guests at a German hotel got a dose of chlorine when a warning about dangerous levels never reached staff. The incident, first reported by German broadcaster WDR, happened on Friday at Hotel Ling Bao, part of the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, Germany, where a malfunctioning automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the swimming pool. The hotel's monitoring system spotted the problem and emailed staff a warning about the excessive chlorine levels. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Outlook service was caught up in a global outage, meaning the warning never arrived. Brühl Fire Department said the problem started when a technical fault caused the pool's dosing equipment to pump in more chlorine than it should have. Chlorine gas then escaped into the swimming area, leaving guests needing medical attention. Paramedics checked over 15 people at the hotel, and five were taken to hospital. Four suffered minor injuries, while one was moderately injured and needed further treatment. The fire department sent about 40 personnel to the scene, and crews spent roughly two hours dealing with the incident. The incident came as Microsoft was battling a major outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and dragged well into Friday. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services were knocked offline, leaving businesses unable to access email and documents. The disruption wasn't confined to office workers unable to check their inboxes, with hospitals, police forces, and government departments reporting problems accessing the Microsoft services they use for day-to-day operations. Redmond has since blamed the outage on a bug introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade . It sat there until a later network change set it off, and the failures then spread across the company's infrastructure. Microsoft ruled out both cybercriminals and AI as culprits, and has issued the customary apology. At Phantasialand, though, a broken inbox was the least of anyone's worries. The chlorine dosing equipment went haywire independently of Microsoft's troubles, but the email warning staff about the problem apparently never arrived. Whether the hotel had a backup alarm, or anything capable of shutting off the chlorine supply automatically, remains unanswered. Why a hotel would rely on Outlook to deliver warnings about dangerous chlorine levels is anyone's guess. Email can be delayed, filtered into spam, or simply disappear when Microsoft's infrastructure throws a tantrum, none of which is particularly helpful when you've got a pool with guests breathing in noxious gas. ®

item.title: Sweden’s H100 Taps Coinbase Prime and Deribit for Its 3,506 Bitcoin Treasury as It Courts Family Offices
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Sweden’s H100 Taps Coinbase Prime and Deribit for Its 3,506 Bitcoin Treasury as It Courts Family Offices Swedish bitcoin treasury company H100 Group said Monday it will use Coinbase Prime and the Deribit derivatives exchange for custody, trading and financing of its roughly 3,506 BTC, a move it says supports both its bitcoin-per-share goal and a push to serve wealthy investors. H100, which trades on Stockholm’s NGM Nordic SME under the ticker H100, announced the partnership in a release Monday morning. The company and its subsidiaries will use Coinbase and Deribit, which Coinbase owns, for custody, trading and financing, it said. H100 valued its holdings at about SEK 2.3 billion, or $226 million, based on a bitcoin price of $64,600 on Nov. 15. It also has about SEK 219 million ($22 million) in outstanding convertible loans that carry 0% interest, mature on July 9, 2030, and equal less than 10% of the stated value of its bitcoin. The release did not disclose fees, collateral terms or borrowing limits. It also didn’t say whether H100 has drawn on any financing, how much of its bitcoin will sit with Coinbase, or whether it is moving coins from another custodian. Prime brokerage for a bitcoin balance sheet H100 described Coinbase’s offering as the crypto version of a bank’s prime brokerage desk, bringing custody, financing and trade execution under one roof. The trading itself will be run in-house. PDI AS, a wholly owned trading and technology unit, builds the software and trading systems used to manage H100’s bitcoin, and the company said those tools operate “with protecting H100’s Bitcoin holdings as the first priority.” “This partnership gives H100 stronger tools for our own balance sheet, and we use them on our own Bitcoin first,” Executive Chairman Sander Andersen said. “Bitcoin per share remains the measure we run the Company by, and these tools are there to help us deliver on it, not to add risk.” Andersen added that this is “the first of several” partnerships, “and the next is already under way.” He did not name the next partner. Lauren Abendschein, head of institutional sales at Coinbase, said bitcoin treasury companies “have grown into an established part of our institutional client base,” and that their priorities are custody, “liquidity when the market moves, and financing against the same balance sheet.” From health tech to family-office ambitions The second goal is bigger. H100 said it wants to become what majority shareholder Geir Harald Hansen, in a June 11 letter to shareholders, called “a leading European alternative and digital asset manager.” It will start with family offices and high-net-worth individuals looking for a partner on bitcoin investments and financing, and said it will share details as products launch. H100 began as a health-tech company before adopting a bitcoin treasury strategy in 2025. It agreed in January to buy Swiss treasury firm Future Holdings and closed that deal in February. item.title: Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
item.description: Mercedes-Benz provided flights from Washington, DC, to San Francisco and accommodation so Ars could try its new driver assistance systems. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year , the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive . Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel. While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak. “Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines. item.title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
item.description: null The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut. Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9). The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated . (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.) For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated. The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service. The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future. Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur , the successor to the venerable Atlas V. Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit. The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef .

item.title: Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help
item.description: A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations. Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3. In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report . This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement. The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. “Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report. The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups. In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN , CyberStrikeAI , HexStrike AI , and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector. “We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®

item.title: Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric
item.description: Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric. Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth. “What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg. Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity. With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules. If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs. Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity. As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely. The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money. In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5. item.title: Strive (ASST) Buys 251 Bitcoin for $17.5 Million as Shares Drop 10% Premarket
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Strive (ASST) Buys 251 Bitcoin for $17.5 Million as Shares Drop 10% Premarket Strive bought another 251 bitcoin last week for $17.5 million at an average of $69,853 per coin, Chairman and CEO Matthew Cole posted Monday, lifting total holdings to 43,404 BTC. “Strive acquired 251 $BTC for $17.5M at an average cost of $69,853 per bitcoin, bringing total holdings to ₿43,404,” Cole wrote. A Monday 8-K filing shows the purchases ran from Nov. 7 through Nov. 13, inclusive of fees and expenses, and took the Dallas company’s stack up from 43,153 bitcoin a week earlier. Cole said Strive raised $10 million through its SATS at-the-market program. The filing puts that total at $10.02 million in gross proceeds from the sale of 104,478 shares of the company’s 15% Series A perpetual preferred stock. Strive sold no Class A common shares and no shares of its variable-rate SATA preferred during the week. Cash and cash equivalents fell $22.3 million to $465.3 million as of Nov. 13. Cole also posted a preferred dividend coverage figure of 133 months and an amplification ratio of 76%, two metrics the 8-K does not break out. The 251-coin add is larger than the 29 bitcoin Strive bought the prior week at an average of $75,721 and the 124 bitcoin it bought in late October at $80,526, but it remains a fraction of the October sprint that built the stack. Holdings stood at 28,000 bitcoin on Sept. 30 before Strive acquired 15,124 coins between Oct. 1 and Oct. 30, including a 6,182-coin buy . The company closed a registered offering of 7 million SATS shares on Oct. 20 for about $609 million in net proceeds and later lined up a $1 billion SATS at-the-market program, the facilities that have funded the larger purchases. Effective common shares outstanding were unchanged at 127,331,109. SATS shares outstanding rose to 7,141,037, while SATA remained at 14,030,176. Strive still holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s variable-rate STRC preferred, marked at a fair value of $50.5 million as of Nov. 13. On Nov. 12, the board raised the regular dividend rate on SATA to 13.25% for periods beginning Dec. 1 and declared daily December cash dividends of $0.0502 a share on SATA and $0.0569 a share on SATS, which continues to carry a 15% rate. Those daily payments total $1.1044 a share on SATA and $1.2518 a share on SATS for the full month. Strive shares drop in premarket trading Strive’s Class A shares fell around 10% in Monday premarket trading to $19.34 as of 8:45 a.m. ET, from Friday’s close of $21.36. The move tracks a broader selloff in bitcoin-linked stocks. Strategy, the largest public corporate holder, was down 8.1% in premarket trading to $102.60 as of 8:45 a.m. ET, from Friday’s close of $111.62. ASST has already given back a large share of its October run. The stock closed Oct. 21 at $30.75 and Oct. 30 at $22.19. item.title: Bitcoin Price Trades Near $64,000 After Weekend Plunge to $62,000
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Trades Near $64,000 After Weekend Plunge to $62,000 Bitcoin price traded near $64,000 on Monday morning, down about 2% from Sunday, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The world’s largest cryptocurrency is trying to hold its ground after a weekend plunge to $62,000, as tech stocks slid ahead of Nvidia’s earnings and traders braced for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month. The selling that broke Friday’s low on Saturday morning did not stop there. Bitcoin slipped under $64,000 Saturday afternoon and dropped below $62,000 in the 8 p.m. ET hour on some exchanges, its lowest level since July 14. It bounced back above $64,800 within the hour and reached about $66,100 early Sunday before sellers returned. The bitcoin price has spent most of the past day between $64,000 and $65,000. The slide has been punishing for leveraged traders. About $2 billion of crypto positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period during the weekend, the vast majority of them long bets. Bitcoin is now down 17% in November and has posted six straight weekly losses. Tech stocks and rate fears weigh on the bitcoin price Stock futures offered little help on Monday. Contracts on the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.5% and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.7%, while Nvidia fell 3% in premarket trading. Investors weighed a Financial Times report that former CEO Jensen Huang and his allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him, a week after his resignation sent bitcoin below $72,000 . Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, and options markets imply an earnings-day move of about 7% in either direction, Pepperstone’s Chris Weston told Reuters. Bitcoin has traded in step with chip stocks for much of the past week, so a weak report could add to the pressure. Rates remain the other weight on the bitcoin price. Traders fully price a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s December meeting, with odds of a half-point move near 8%, CME FedWatch data show. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12% on Monday after jumping 29 basis points last week, and higher yields have lifted the dollar to its strongest level since April 2025. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks in San Francisco later Monday, and minutes from the last Fed meeting are due Wednesday. Strategy slides as ETF outflows stretch to seven sessions Bitcoin-linked stocks fell with the coin. Strategy (MSTR) was down 8% in premarket trading and Strive (ASST) fell 9%. Strategy is also facing index-fund selling after MSCI removed it from its USA index , forcing index funds to sell by Nov. 30. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed another $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows, bringing losses since Nov. 5 to about $1.91 billion. That run follows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bleeding $2 billion over nine straight sessions. item.title: Strategy (MSTR) Adds 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 Million as It Spends $228 Million Buying Back Preferred Stock
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Strategy (MSTR) Adds 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 Million as It Spends $228 Million Buying Back Preferred Stock Strategy bought another 485 bitcoin last week. A Monday 8-K filing shows the Saylor-led firm spent $33.4 million at an average of $68,887 per coin between November 9 and November 15, lifting total holdings to 850,849 BTC bought for $64.20 billion at an average of $75,452. The coins were funded with net proceeds from MSTR common stock sales. Strategy sold 2,087,040 shares for $244.7 million, put $33.4 million into bitcoin, used $206.3 million of those proceeds to buy back its STRC preferred and parked $5.0 million in USD Cash. No preferred stock was sold under the ATM during the week. The STRC buyback was larger than that ATM slice. Strategy retired 2,282,510 STRC shares for $228.1 million, funding the other $21.8 million with interest earned on its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments. It still has $332.2 million left under its preferred repurchase program and $1.0 billion under its MSTR buyback authorization, with about $18.1 billion of MSTR still available under the ATM. The $228.1 million preferred repurchase was nearly seven times the $33.4 million bitcoin spend. The 485-coin add was also less than half the 1,036 bitcoin Strategy bought the week before. BREAKING: Public companies Strategy and Strive bought over $47 million worth of Bitcoin during this dip Strategy: 485 BTC Strive: 251 BTC pic.twitter.com/alNNfxbQY2 — Bitcoin Magazine (@BitcoinMagazine) November 16, 2026 A deeper hole under the treasury The filing lands as the spot bitcoin price sits well below Strategy’s average cost. At the time of writing it trades near $64,100, about 15% under the $75,452 basis, leaving the stack roughly $9.7 billion underwater on paper. A week earlier, the same treasury was only modestly below cost after bitcoin slipped under $75,000. The new coins do not close that gap. They were bought at $68,887, above today’s price but well below last week’s $79,012 average, and they shaved the company’s overall cost basis by only $4, to $75,452 from $75,456. Strategy now holds more than 4% of bitcoin’s 21 million supply cap. The pace of buying has slowed as the firm has put more ATM cash into preferred buybacks than into bitcoin, a pattern that also marked the prior week’s purchase. Between June 30 and August 10, Strategy sold bitcoin in four consecutive filings to fund preferred dividends and STRC buybacks before flipping back to accumulation. Dividends stay at 12% as the reserve is drawn Strategy used $18.9 million of its USD Reserve during the week to pay preferred dividends. As of November 15, the reserve stood at $4.75 billion and USD Cash at $151.2 million. On November 15, the company said it will keep the regular dividend rate on STRC at 12.00% for record dates in December. Daily STRC dividends for the month total $1.00 per share. item.title: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
item.description: null We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets. But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic. "In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule." As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't." Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions. 130 million pieces of debris are currently estimated to be orbiting Earth. (Image credit: ESA) In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome , with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth . Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth. What is the Astra Carta? The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility. Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies . The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart. "I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022. item.title: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
item.description: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators. NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size. Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.” “It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained. Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained. In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems. A compute chameleon LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations. These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements. A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.” There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.” CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads.

item.title: How many times are you paying to store the same file?
item.description: Pick any busy project folder and count the copies. There's one on the file server, one in a cloud bucket and one on each laptop that needed it at a usable speed. If a team got fed up with sync and built its own workaround, there's another in there too. The storage bill pays for every one of them. The Register and LucidLink are hosting senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November to compare how they're bringing that number down. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. Request a place Nobody keeps duplicates for fun. They're what people do when files have to move between sites faster than sync allows. Every copy IT can't see into is a security question as well as a cost, so the duplicates you don't know about matter most. What the table wants to hear is how others got the copies down without ripping out storage they've already paid for, or the governance built around it. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, so people say what worked and what didn't. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers. Nobody presents. Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited. Request a place at the 24 November dinner Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally. item.title: SpaceX catches Starship on the first try
item.description: SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage returning from orbit on its first attempt, but the Super Heavy booster ended its flight in an explosion after recovery was aborted. The catch was a remarkable achievement: Starship returned to the same launch tower it had left almost a day earlier, settling into its giant mechanical arms. Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left. Many more development flights remain before SpaceX can deliver its promised fully reusable launch system. NASA's Space Shuttle came close, but the large external tank was expended with every launch, and the orbiters never matched the cadence SpaceX reckons it can achieve with Starship. SpaceX boss Elon Musk admitted that "many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)." Cadence will be key if Starship is going to meet NASA's needs for the Artemis missions. Somewhere between 6 and 22 launches (depending on who you ask) will be required for a lunar mission, and SpaceX has yet to demonstrate in-space propellant transfer between vehicles. Next year's Artemis III mission also calls for docking tests between NASA's Orion spacecraft and a test version of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System (HLS) in low Earth orbit. The booster fumble shouldn't obscure what the engineering teams achieved. Now comes the small matter of doing it again – preferably with both stages intact. ®

item.title: Datacenters' share of UK planning applications nearly triples in three years
item.description: Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions. The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK. Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities. The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000. The figures show that applications for building new server halls are about as high as they have been over the past decade, and close to their recent peak as a share of all applications. Even so, the application numbers don't show the dramatic jump that the steady stream of bit barn announcements might suggest. Nor do they tell us how many facilities are actually being built. Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected. But it didn't publish the AI Opportunities Action Plan , which recommended "AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning to speed up datacenter builds, until the start of 2025. Plota links the rise to datacenters being recognized as critical national infrastructure (CNI) in September 2024, and a December 2024 update to the planning framework that told councils to identify suitable sites for them. The facilities are getting larger. One site being built for Equinix near London's M25 motorway will feature three data halls with more than 250 MW capacity, while another planned for Havering in East London could go up to 600 MW. Both were billed as being among Europe's largest campuses. According to Plota, just 3.3 percent of datacenter applications decided between 2016 and 2024 were refused, against 11.3 percent across all applications. The government has also overturned some local council refusals, controversially, as at a site near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire last year. Slough leads Plota's tally of applications since 2016 with 28, followed by Tower Hamlets in East London with 16, Leeds with 12, and West Northamptonshire with 11. Developers in England can also ask ministers to bring qualifying datacenter projects into the nationally significant infrastructure planning regime , shifting the consent decision from the council to central government. Projects taking that route fall outside Plota's council-based figures. A recent report found UK ministers met with representatives from 137 different businesses between July 2024 and June 2026 to discuss datacenters, while there were no meetings with environmental or community groups about them. ®

item.title: Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.
item.description: In August, Amazon announced plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “ nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026 ." Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace. For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator's line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones. The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia. ” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media. item.title: Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia
item.description: Elon Musk and a bunch of Silicon Valley heavyweights want Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and they've decided an online petition is the way to make it happen. An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out. "For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes. "Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now." Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce. However, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it. The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12 , ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the company while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis , with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest. Huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times , the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach Chin

item.title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix
item.description: Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the iss

item.title: NASA's interstellar Voyager 1 probe is about to reach 1 light-day from Earth after nearly 50 years in space
item.description: null Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth. NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating." During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4. Going the distance Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2 . NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/KSC) A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet. Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s . The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did. Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan , executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane. An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA

item.title: Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet
item.description: Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Like most distros, Omaxian is available as an ISO file you can install and use. Alternatively, Omaxian Shell can be installed on an existing Debian-family distro without replacing the underlying operating system. The OS release is codenamed "Trans-Siberian Shaman," and the GitHub project repository shows work going back just a few weeks. No LLM coding assistant is credited on the project page, but we looked inside some of the test scripts, and as well as being verbose and hard to read, they also credit "Grok Bot." Omarchy itself is of course built with LLM assistance, and as we reported last month , so is the new Daemonarchy FreeBSD-based desktop project. Omaxian is styled after Omarchy, and it includes some of the same tools – and optional support for LLMs – but it's not based on the same tech. Instead of Arch, it's based on Devuan 6, the current version of the systemd-free fork of Debian. Omaxian eschews Hyprland, and indeed Wayland altogether: it opts for an X11 tiling window manager – in this case, i3 . i3 first appeared in 2009, so it's been around much longer than Hyprland. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win. The window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too. We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. item.title: We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone
item.description: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. item.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
item.description: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

item.title: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
item.description: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light . Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode . Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when.
